Each Palace simulation class has a class-level `simulation_drc()` that tells a
layout repository whether that simulation can model and mesh its layout, and
where to fix it when it cannot. It runs in two stages and never meshes:

1. **Geometry stage.** The same preparation and geometry build that the class's
   `mesh()` runs. A layout that cannot be built is refused with the error the
   build raises.
2. **Meshing stage.** Only a model that built goes on. The check measures every
   edge and face of the built model and reports those too fine for the mesher,
   each with its place in µm, its size, its owner and its fix. A refusal raises
   `SimulationDrcError`.

A layout that passes both stages returns a `SimulationDrcReport`, which lists
the meshing-stage warnings. Each class's `mesh()` runs the same meshing stage
on the model it builds, before the mesher starts; see
[The same check inside `mesh()`](#the-same-check-inside-mesh).

The geometry stage catches layout defects that stop modeling: malformed shapes,
overlaps, tiny misalignments, wrong semantic declarations, port sheets that do
not sit where they should, and Surface EPR bands that do not fit the drawn
gaps. It does not predict the final simulation geometry. The patterns SCGSim is
tested on are listed in [Supported Geometry](../reference/supported-geometry.qmd), and the
known failures with their layout fixes in
[Known Geometry Problems](../reference/known-geometry-problems.qmd). The rules the check
enforces, and who owns each failure, are on [Supported Scope](../reference/supported-scope.qmd).

## Build the plan the simulation is given {#build-the-plan}

The check takes the `GeometryPlan` the simulation will be given, before
`prepare()`, so the model it checks is the model that simulation builds. Build
the plan once in the layout repository and pass it to each check: six lines.

```python
from scgsim.geometry import GeometryPlan
from scgsim.palace import EigenmodeSim

plan = GeometryPlan(component=component, root_id="chip", layer_stack=layer_stack, material_records=material_records, coupon_padding_um=0.0)
plan.set_nets({"Ground": ("chip/D0_TOP_GROUND_PLANE", ...), ...})
plan.set_vacuum_region((0.0, 0.0, 1000.0))  # when the layer stack has no VACUUM_REGION
plan.set_rectangular_junctions([...])  # when the layout has rectangular junctions
plan.set_surface_epr(surface_epr_specs)  # when the simulations compute Surface EPR
report = EigenmodeSim.simulation_drc(plan, route="A")

print(report.render_text())  # the warnings, if any
```

SCGSim does not depend on a PDK, so the layout repository passes its layer
stack and material records to the plan. The Palace check needs
`scgsim[palace]` installed. For an assembly, register each instance with
`plan.register_instance("chip/device", reference)` before `set_nets`, a parent
before its children (`chip/device` before `chip/device/pads`).

The check uses the plan as the simulation uses it and adds nothing to it:

- **Nets.** The plan's `set_nets`, each member a qualified Entity ID under the
  plan's root. Without Nets no conductor has one, so any two conductors that
  touch are refused as a different-Net contact. That refuses every flip-chip
  layout whose indium bumps join the two ground planes, until both planes and
  every bump are in one Ground net. A contact between conductors of two
  different Nets is refused either way.
- **Vacuum.** The plan's own: the stack's `VACUUM_REGION`, or the plan's
  `set_vacuum_region`. A plan with neither is refused with the error the
  simulation raises for it. `(0, 0, 1000)` µm is the setting layouts are
  tested and used with: the vacuum ends at the layout's planar extent and
  reaches 1000 µm below and above, so the metal has air faces for `MA` and
  `SA` bands.
- **Surface EPR.** The plan's `set_surface_epr(specs)`, the specs the
  simulations will use (the [Eigenmode contract](../reference/specs/palace-eigenmode.qmd#surface-epr-margins)
  lists their keys). Their margins are cut into the geometry as bands, so a
  layout that cannot carry them is refused here too. Bands are cut only on the
  faces the specs select, so a layout with no such face passes with no bands;
  a plan without specs gets no bands.
- **Coupon padding, port sheets and rectangular junctions.** As the plan
  declares them.

The plan you pass is left as it was. A first argument that is not a
`GeometryPlan`, such as the Component or `plan.prepare()`, is refused with the
plan to build. [What the check uses](#what-the-check-uses) lists what each
class adds of its own.

Call the check from the repository's tests and while the layout is being
drawn. Pass `route` and `approximation_profile` with the route the simulations
will use: they are the arguments of
[`set_route`](../reference/specs/physical-representation.qmd#palace-caller-profile), with
its defaults and refusals. Without them the check is Route B; `route="A"` alone
uses the `thin_film` profile, and `route="A"` with a `substrate_face` or
`metal_gap_equivalent` profile uses that profile and its `film_bindings`. A
profile the plan's films do not fit is refused by the geometry build, with the
error `mesh()` raises. Route C is not a Palace route and is refused, as
`set_route` refuses it; a refusal of the route or the profile names the
`simulation_drc` call. A layout meant for both routes calls the check once for
each.

The check builds the geometry and does not mesh or solve, so it can be repeated
as the layout changes. The geometry stage stops at its first refusal; the
meshing stage lists every finding at once. Read the message, fix the layout,
and run it again. [When something fails](../reference/supported-scope.qmd#when-something-fails)
gives the owner and the next action for each error.

A geometry-stage refusal can also come from a defect in SGB rather than from
the layout. If the message does not match the layout you drew, report it to
SCGSim.

## Which check to run {#which-check-to-run}

Each simulation class checks its own pipeline, so run the check of each
simulation the cell is meant for:

| The cell is meant for | The call |
|---|---|
| Palace Eigenmode | `scgsim.palace.EigenmodeSim.simulation_drc(plan, route=...)` |
| Palace Electrostatic | `scgsim.palace.ElectrostaticSim.simulation_drc(plan, route=...)` |
| AEDT HFSS Eigenmode | `scgsim.aedt.EigenmodeSim.simulation_drc(plan, modeling=...)` |
| AEDT HFSS Driven Terminal or Q3D | no check: `prepare_hfss_driven_from_geometry` and `prepare_q3d_from_geometry` run the same steps before AEDT starts, and refuse there |

One check stands for another in one case only:

- **Palace `EigenmodeSim` and `ElectrostaticSim`**, on the same plan, route,
  profile and specs: when the plan has no port sheet, both build the same
  model, so a pass of one is a pass of the other. With port sheets they
  differ: `EigenmodeSim` cuts each sheet to the rectangle between its two
  conductors, as a lumped port, while `ElectrostaticSim` keeps the sheet as
  drawn. Neither pass then implies the other.
- **Palace and AEDT** never stand for each other. They build different routes
  (Palace A or B; AEDT A with finite bodies kept as solids, or C), and their
  second stages differ: Palace refuses edges and faces too fine for its mesher,
  which AEDT does not check, and AEDT refuses what its import cannot realize
  (the Region box, two IDs that share one AEDT name, an untreated port sheet),
  which Palace does not check.

So no single check represents the others. For a cell meant for several
simulations, run each one's check on the one plan:

```python
import scgsim.aedt
import scgsim.palace

checks = [
    (scgsim.palace.EigenmodeSim, {"route": "B"}),
    (scgsim.palace.ElectrostaticSim, {"route": "B"}),
    (scgsim.aedt.EigenmodeSim, {"modeling": "solid"}),
]
for simulation, options in checks:
    report = simulation.simulation_drc(plan, **options)
    print(f"{simulation.__module__}.{simulation.__name__}")
    print(report.render_text())
```

A refusal raises, so the loop stops at the first class that refuses the plan.

## What the meshing stage reports {#what-the-meshing-stage-reports}

The mesher cannot fill an edge or face of a few grid steps with usable
tetrahedra: it refines around it and new bad elements appear. Such geometry is
valid, so the geometry stage passes it. The meshing stage reads only the
sidecar of the built model and sorts each such edge or face into a class:

| Class | What is measured | Found when | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | the column gap of a wall face: the length of the outline edge it stands on between its two side-wall columns, measured along the edge (an arc's length for a curved wall) | below 10 grid steps | refuse |
| B | the width 2A/P of a horizontal face (A its area, P its perimeter), or its sharpest corner | below 10 grid steps, or sharper than 1° | refuse |
| C | the length of a horizontal edge that bounds no wall | below 25 grid steps | warn |

Limits are in grid steps, so they scale with the model grid: on a 1 nm grid,
class A finds a wall face narrower than 10 nm. Findings give µm beside them.
The limits and actions are held in `scgsim.meshing.FineStructureLimits`.

Every band you request must be at least as wide as the class B limit, 10 grid
steps. The first band is as wide as the first margin, and each next band is the
difference of two margins: `[0.5, 1.0]` µm gives two bands of 0.5 µm. A
narrower band is refused with `ValueError` before anything is built; the
message names the spec (or the conductor of `inset_margins_by_entity_um`), the
band, its width in µm and grid steps, and the limit. Widen the margins. A band
right at the limit can still be refused as class B where it is cut open, for
example at the die edge: the width 2A/P of a piece that ends is a little less
than the band's width. Choose bands wider than the limit.

::: {.callout-tip title="Keep each conductor's core wide"}
With Surface-EPR bands, keep each conductor's core, the region beyond its
largest margin, much wider than its bands. Where a conductor narrows to exactly
twice its largest margin, the bands meet down its middle: the model is still
the exact erosion and meshes, with class C warnings for the short band edges at
that neck. A little wider, the conductor keeps a sliver of core that class B
refuses; see [Surface-EPR margins](../reference/supported-scope.qmd#rules-margins).
:::

Each finding names its stage, class, measure and size, the SGB entity and its
physical group, the layout objects and band requests it comes from and the
layers those objects were drawn on, its location and box in µm, why the mesher
fails on it, and the fix. Its owner
comes from the lineage the sidecar records:

- **layout**: the feature is bounded only by source curves, or it is a band
  curve within the band's widest margin of such a feature, which the band
  repeats. Whoever draws the layout fixes it. A fine edge or face that SGB did
  not cause is a layout problem: SCGSim reports it and does not repair it.
- **erosion**: band offsets of two source edges that are not neighbours meet
  here, as when a conductor is barely wider than twice the margin. The exact
  erosion has this structure. Change the inset margins given to
  `plan.set_surface_epr` or the conductor's width. Also a short band edge that
  offsets a straight source edge shorter than its band margin, such as one
  chord of a curve drawn as a polygon: the fix names that source edge, where
  it runs and how long it is.
  Declare the arc exactly, or draw it with longer chords.
- **sgb**: a band curve where the source has no fine structure. This is an SGB
  defect; report it to SCGSim with the finding. The layout needs no change.

Two source edges are neighbours when they share a vertex, including the last
and first edges of a closed outline.

## The same check inside `mesh()` {#the-same-check-inside-mesh}

`EigenmodeSim.mesh()` and `ElectrostaticSim.mesh()` build the geometry, run
this meshing stage on the model they built, and only then start the mesher:

- **A refusing finding** raises `SimulationDrcError` before any meshing. Its
  `report` holds the same findings `simulation_drc` gives for the same model.
  The built geometry stays in the output folder, and no mesh path is returned.
- **Warnings only** do not stop `mesh()`; it meshes the model as usual.

`mesh()` checks the model of the plan and of the simulation's own settings,
such as its route and ports, while `simulation_drc` checks
the model of the plan it is given, on the route it is given, with the inputs of
[What the check uses](#what-the-check-uses). For the same plan, the same route
and profile build the same model in both; when the two models differ, so can
their findings.

`mesh()` also reports in the same terms when its repair loop stops without a
clean mesh. The error and the text quality report first give what the meshing
stage found anywhere in the model: for each class and measure, the number of
findings and whether they refuse or warn, the smallest size in µm and grid
steps, the count per owner, and the smallest finding in full with its owner and
fix. Fine structure can cost the repair loop rounds wherever it is, so these
findings can matter even at a place that has none of its own. The JSON quality
report lists every finding under `meshing_stage`. Then come the µm locations of
the remaining bad elements (`stop_places`) and the findings at those places,
with their owner and fix. A place is the reach of the refinement the loop
applied there. A place with no finding is SCGSim's to answer for; when the
model has findings elsewhere, act on those as well.

## What the check uses {#what-the-check-uses}

The plan is used as the simulation uses it
([Build the plan the simulation is given](#build-the-plan)). The rest is the
call's or fixed:

- the route and profile given as `route` and `approximation_profile`, as
  `set_route` takes them, and Route B when they are not given;
- for `EigenmodeSim`, every authored port sheet of the plan as a lumped port
  with a fixed inductance, which does not change the geometry;
- for `ElectrostaticSim`, no terminals, which are not needed before meshing.

A vacuum padded by (0, 0, 1000) µm ends at the layout's planar extent, so draw
what sets the extent: the die outline or a ground plane. A conductor that
reaches the extent only at a point, such as a lone round pad with nothing drawn
around it, is refused with `NonManifoldError`;
[A conductor that touches the boundary at one point](../reference/known-geometry-problems.qmd#boundary-point-pinch)
explains why and what to draw.

`simulation_drc()` writes into a temporary folder and removes it. The geometry
stage adds no rules of its own, so its error is the one that class's `mesh()`
raises for the same plan and settings. The meshing stage's rules are the
classes above.

::: {.callout-note title="What a pass means"}
A pass means the model of the plan, built on the route and profile checked
with the inputs above, was accepted and has no edge or face that a
meshing-stage class refuses; it does not say how many bands were cut. It does
not promise that other settings will model: another route or profile,
Electrostatic terminals or lumped supports. To check a specific set-up, run that simulation's own
`mesh()`. Nor does a pass promise a clean mesh: the meshing-stage classes guard
against fine structure, and `mesh()` can still stop with `MeshRepairError`,
which then names the places where it stopped.
:::

## The check of the AEDT Eigenmode simulation {#aedt-eigenmode-check}

`scgsim.aedt.EigenmodeSim` builds its model from the same SGB geometry and
imports its STEP into HFSS, so it has its own class-level `simulation_drc()`.
It checks the geometry half of that simulation's own pipeline, everything
before AEDT starts, and needs no AEDT:

1. the plan's SGB model on the route `modeling` realizes: `"thin_film"` is
   Route A (each conductor a sheet), `"solid"` is Route C (each conductor a
   solid of its film's thickness);
2. the STEP export and its import guard, the Region box against the plan's
   `VACUUM_REGION`, and the AEDT names of Nets and RLCs (two IDs that become
   one AEDT name are refused, naming both);
3. the import's first step: every port sheet's boundary on the guarded faces;
4. the selection of every Surface-EPR row on the faces the import will hold.

```python
from scgsim.aedt import EigenmodeSim

report = EigenmodeSim.simulation_drc(plan, modeling="solid")  # or "thin_film"; no default
print(report.render_text())  # geometry stage: passed
```

It takes the same plan as the Palace check
([Build the plan the simulation is given](#build-the-plan)), with `modeling` in
place of `route` and `approximation_profile`: Route C is checked here, and the
Palace classes keep refusing it. A layout meant for both modelings calls the
check once for each. It needs `scgsim[aedt]` installed (the STEP export uses
OCP). AEDT's Region is the plan's vacuum box, so the plan must have a vacuum: a
plan without one is refused with the error `prepare_handoff()` raises.

A step that refuses raises the error that step raises in the simulation,
unchanged, so read it as you read a refusal of `prepare_handoff()`. AEDT
meshes the model itself, so there is no meshing stage: the
`SimulationDrcReport` of `scgsim.aedt` has the geometry stage only. Every port
sheet of the plan gets a parallel inductance, which the geometry never reads,
so the import treats it. A rectangular junction of the plan is in the model
checked: its sheet is cut to the rectangle between its two terminals, as the
simulation cuts it, and gets that inductance too. A junction's inductance,
capacitance and width do not shape the geometry; `prepare_handoff()` compares
its width and Nets with the sheet before AEDT starts. A pass means that model
can be built and imported. It does not promise the other `modeling`, nor that
AEDT meshes or solves the model; run that simulation's `prepare_handoff()` and
its AEDT run for that.

HFSS Driven Terminal and Q3D C/G have no simulation class:
`prepare_hfss_driven_from_geometry` and `prepare_q3d_from_geometry` build the
model with `prepare_sgb_model(...)` and run the import's first step on it
before they write the handoff, so a model the import cannot realize is refused
there, without AEDT.
